New Section Added: Genotype-Phenotype Relationships
A comprehensive analysis of the relationship between beta-lactamase genes and antimicrobial susceptibility has been added to the report.

What Was Added

Section: “Genotype-Phenotype Relationships”
Location: Between “Resistance Genotypes” and “Capsular Type-Resistance Associations”

Content Overview

1. Beta-lactamase Gene Burden Analysis

Distribution of additional genes (excluding universal KPC-31)
50% of isolates have no additional beta-lactamases
Up to 4 additional genes per isolate



2. MIC by Gene Burden

Key Finding: No dose-response relationship
Paradox: 4 genes = lowest median MIC (12 mg/L)
0 genes = wide MIC range (4-644 mg/L, 161-fold!)



3. Individual Gene Effects

Median MIC for isolates carrying each gene
blaSHV-11 carriers: highest median (256 mg/L)
Context-dependent effects observed



4. Clone-Specific Patterns

ST307 Paradox: Most genes (CTX-M-15 + SHV-28) but LOWEST MIC
ST101: Few genes but HIGHEST MIC (256 mg/L)
ST512: IncX3 plasmid-borne KPC-31
ST147: Multiple genes, high MIC as expected



5. Gene Combination Effects

CTX-M-15 + SHV-28: Highest synergy (256 mg/L)
CTX-M-15 + TEM: Lower MIC (12 mg/L)
Context-dependent, non-additive effects



6. Mechanistic Insights (Tabbed Panels)

KPC-31 Dominance: Universal but variable expression
Synergistic Effects: Epistatic interactions
Clone Effects: Genetic background critical
Clinical Implications: Both WGS + MIC needed

Visualizations Added

Bar Chart: Median MIC for each individual gene
Scatter Plot: Clone-specific genotype-phenotype relationships
Multiple Tables:

Gene burden distribution

Key Discoveries Highlighted

🔬 Major Finding
Complex, non-linear genotype-phenotype relationships: - Same genes → different phenotypes in different clones - More genes ≠ higher resistance - Clone identity is critical


⚠️ The ST307 Paradox

Most additional genes: CTX-M-15 (10/16), SHV-28 (13/16)
Lowest median MIC: 18 mg/L
Hypothesis: Chromosomal KPC-31 with lower expression



✓ Clinical Relevance

Genotype alone insufficient for treatment decisions
Phenotypic testing (MIC) essential
Integration needed: WGS + MIC + MLST

Overview
This section examines the relationship between beta-lactamase gene carriage (resistome) and antimicrobial susceptibility phenotypes (MIC values) across the 42 KPC-31-producing isolates. While all isolates carry blaKPC-31, they exhibit considerable diversity in additional beta-lactamase genes, which may contribute to variations in resistance profiles.

Beta-lactamase Gene Distribution

Interpretation: The pronounced species-specific clustering suggests that beta-lactamase gene acquisition follows species-adapted evolutionary pathways. This likely reflects differences in mobile genetic element compatibility (e.g., plasmid host range) and/or divergent selective pressures between the two species in clinical and laboratory environments.

Genotype-Phenotype Associations

Beta-lactamase Genes and Antibiotic Susceptibility
Analysis of associations between individual beta-lactamase genes and MIC values for key antibiotics revealed several notable patterns:


Code
# Perform statistical analysis for major genes
major_genes <- names(gene_prev_sorted)[gene_prev_sorted >= 5]
gene_mic_comparisons <- list()

for(gene in major_genes) {
  key_antibiotics_analysis <- c("CAZ_AVI", "CAZ", "FEP", "ATM", "C/T", "PIP__TAZ", "MER")
  
  for(abx in key_antibiotics_analysis) {
    if(abx %in% colnames(analysis_data)) {
      with_gene <- analysis_data[[abx]][analysis_data[[gene]] == 1]
      without_gene <- analysis_data[[abx]][analysis_data[[gene]] == 0]
      
      with_gene <- with_gene[!is.na(with_gene)]
      without_gene <- without_gene[!is.na(without_gene)]
      
      if(length(with_gene) >= 3 & length(without_gene) >= 3) {
        median_with <- median(with_gene)
        median_without <- median(without_gene)
        
        fold_change <- if(median_without > 0) median_with / median_without else NA
        
        test_result <- wilcox.test(with_gene, without_gene)
        p_val <- test_result$p.value
        
        # Store results if notable (p < 0.1 or FC > 2 or FC < 0.5)
        if(!is.na(p_val) && (p_val < 0.1 || (!is.na(fold_change) && (fold_change > 2 || fold_change < 0.5)))) {
          gene_mic_comparisons[[length(gene_mic_comparisons) + 1]] <- list(
            gene = gene,
            antibiotic = abx,
            median_with = median_with,
            median_without = median_without,
            fold_change = fold_change,
            p_value = p_val,
            n_with = length(with_gene),
            n_without = length(without_gene)
          )
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Key Findings:

bla_TEM-1 and CAZ-AVI resistance (p=0.091):

Isolates carrying bla_TEM-1 show 5.1-fold higher CAZ-AVI MICs (median 164 vs 32 mg/L)
Suggests possible synergistic interaction with blaKPC-31 affecting ceftazidime-avibactam susceptibility
This association approaches statistical significance despite small sample size (n=6 with gene)

blaOXA-1 and CAZ-AVI susceptibility (p=0.066):

Isolates with blaOXA-1 show 8.1-fold lower CAZ-AVI MICs (median 18 vs 146 mg/L)
This counterintuitive finding may reflect:

Clonal structure: blaOXA-1-positive isolates may belong to specific lineages with different blaKPC-31 genetic contexts (e.g., different plasmids, promoters, or expression levels)
Gene combinations: These isolates tend to carry multiple beta-lactamases (see quadruple-gene profile below)
Sampling artifact: The small E. coli subset (mostly lab strains) may influence this pattern


blaTEM-1B and aztreonam:

4-fold higher aztreonam MICs in blaTEM-1B-positive isolates
Consistent with the hydrolytic activity of TEM variants on monobactams

Limited carbapenem associations:

ESBL genes (BlaCTXM-15, blaSHV-28) show minimal impact on carbapenem MICs
Carbapenem resistance is predominantly mediated by blaKPC-31








NoteStatistical Power Considerations



Several associations show large effect sizes (fold changes >2) but limited statistical significance due to small sample sizes for rarer genes. P-values between 0.05-0.15 should be considered hypothesis-generating and warrant validation in larger, independent datasets. The paradoxical blaOXA-1 association particularly requires further investigation in a larger cohort with genomic context analysis.

Background and Rationale
A key characteristic of KPC-31-producing isolates is variable carbapenem susceptibility despite universal carriage of the carbapenemase gene. Many KPC-31 isolates show “reversion” to meropenem susceptibility, suggesting that factors beyond blaKPC-31 presence modulate carbapenem resistance. Key Finding:
Isolates carrying ANY TEM beta-lactamase gene show a trend toward higher meropenem MICs:

2-fold higher median MIC (4 vs 2 mg/L, p=0.056)
32.7% lower susceptibility rate (40% vs 72.7% susceptible)

Interpretation:
This association is unlikely to be causal because:

TEM enzymes are narrow-spectrum beta-lactamases that do NOT hydrolyze carbapenems
The association more likely reflects:

Clonal effects: TEM genes may be enriched in clones with higher KPC-31 expression or porin mutations
Co-inheritance patterns: TEM genes on plasmids that also carry other resistance determinants or regulatory factors
Epidemiological clustering: Different circulating strains with variable TEM carriage and carbapenem susceptibility


Clinical Implication:
While TEM genes themselves do not confer carbapenem resistance, their presence may serve as a marker for reduced meropenem susceptibility in KPC-31 isolates. This finding suggests possible clonal transmission of more resistant KPC-31 strains carrying TEM genes and warrants careful MIC testing when TEM genes are detected alongside KPC-31.


Main Findings and Interpretation






ImportantKey Conclusion: Accessory Genes Do NOT Explain Meropenem Susceptibility



The analysis reveals NO association between beta-lactamase gene content and meropenem susceptibility status in KPC-31 isolates:

Gene prevalence: Similar distribution of ESBLs and other beta-lactamases in MER-susceptible vs MER-resistant groups
Gene burden: No difference in total gene count (median 0 in both, p=0.80)
Statistical testing: No genes show significant enrichment in either group (all p≥0.15)

This strongly suggests that the KPC-31 “reversion” to meropenem susceptibility is driven by factors OTHER than accessory beta-lactamase gene content.




Likely Mechanisms of Variable Meropenem Susceptibility
Since accessory beta-lactamase genes do not explain the variability, the meropenem susceptibility likely results from:

Variable KPC-31 expression levels

Transcriptional regulation differences
Plasmid copy number variation
Promoter strength variations

Porin deficiency status

ompK35 and ompK36 mutations
Differential porin expression
Loss vs. partial function

Genetic context of blaKPC-31

Plasmid type and stability
Position relative to mobile elements
Upstream regulatory sequences

Efflux pump activity

AcrAB-TolC expression
Other multidrug efflux systems

Clonal background effects

ST-specific characteristics
Background mutations affecting fitness




Clinical Implications






TipImplications for Clinical Practice and Research



For Clinicians: - Individual susceptibility testing is essential for KPC-31 isolates - Genotypic detection of blaKPC-31 alone cannot predict carbapenem phenotype - ~60% of KPC-31 isolates may remain carbapenem-susceptible - Gene presence/absence data provides limited phenotypic prediction value - TEM gene presence may serve as a marker (not cause) for reduced meropenem susceptibility, warranting careful testing
For Researchers: - Future studies should focus on KPC-31 expression levels and porin status - Whole-genome sequencing with transcriptomics needed to understand mechanism - Plasmid characterization and copy number quantification recommended - Clonal background may be more important than accessory gene content




Recommendations for Future Investigation
To elucidate the mechanisms of variable meropenem susceptibility in KPC-31 isolates:

Quantitative RT-PCR: Measure blaKPC-31 mRNA expression levels
Whole-genome sequencing: Assess ompK35/ompK36 porin gene status
Plasmid analysis: Determine copy number and genetic environment
Promoter sequencing: Analyze blaKPC-31 upstream regulatory regions
Clonal structure analysis: Correlate MLST/cgMLST with phenotype
Protein expression studies: Quantify KPC-31 enzyme levels

Summary and Conclusions

Key Genotype-Phenotype Relationships

Universal KPC-31, variable accessory resistome:

All 42 isolates carry blaKPC-31
55% carry 1-6 additional beta-lactamase genes
Accessory genes show strong species-specificity

Species-specific gene acquisition patterns:

K. pneumoniae preferentially acquires ESBLs (BlaCTXM-15, blaSHV-28, blaOXA-1)
E. coli shows enrichment for OXA-9/18 variants
Reflects species-adapted evolutionary pathways and plasmid compatibility

Complex genotype-phenotype relationships:

bla_TEM-1 associated with higher CAZ-AVI MICs (5.1-fold, p=0.091)
blaOXA-1 paradoxically associated with lower CAZ-AVI MICs (likely clonal effect)
Gene burden does not predict resistance level
Genomic context and clonal background are critical determinants

Clonal vs. polyclonal patterns:

Quadruple-gene K. pneumoniae cluster (n=4) shows homogeneous low CAZ-AVI MICs
KPC-31-only isolates (n=19) show 64-fold MIC variation
Suggests expression-level differences and genetic context effects




Clinical and Research Implications






ImportantKey Messages for Clinical Practice




Genotypic data has limited phenotypic predictive value: The 64-fold CAZ-AVI MIC range (4-644 mg/L) among genetically similar isolates underscores the necessity of direct antimicrobial susceptibility testing for patient management.
CAZ-AVI variability despite universal KPC-31: Clinicians should not assume uniform CAZ-AVI resistance in KPC-31 isolates. Individual testing is required, as 35.7% show high-level resistance (>16 mg/L) while others remain relatively susceptible.
Species trends vs. individual variation: While K. pneumoniae shows trends toward higher beta-lactam MICs due to ESBL co-carriage, within-species variation is substantial enough to preclude species-based treatment decisions.
Limited value of accessory beta-lactamase testing: Knowing additional beta-lactamase gene content provides minimal added predictive value beyond phenotypic testing.





Future Directions

Expression-level analysis:

Quantitative RT-PCR or RNA-seq to measure blaKPC-31 and accessory gene expression
Proteomics to assess functional enzyme levels

Genomic context characterization:

Complete plasmid sequencing to identify genetic environments
Promoter region analysis (blaKPC-31 upstream sequences)
IS element and transposon mapping

Clonal analysis:

Whole-genome sequencing for SNP-based phylogeny
Investigation of the quadruple-gene K. pneumoniae cluster
Assessment of porin mutations and efflux pump variants

Expanded validation:

Test observed associations in larger, geographically diverse cohorts
Include more clinical E. coli isolates (reduce lab strain bias)
Longitudinal studies to assess temporal stability

Mechanistic studies:

Site-directed mutagenesis of blaKPC-31 variants
Fitness cost measurements for multi-gene carriage
In vitro evolution experiments under antibiotic pressure

Beta-lactamase genes examined: 13 (excluding universal blaKPC-31)
Antibiotics tested: 28

title: Genomic and phenotypic characterization of KPC-31-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli: convergence of high-risk clones and complex genotype-phenotype relationships
text:
Background. KPC-31, a single-amino-acid variant of KPC-3, confers resistance to ceftazidime-avibactam (CAZ-AVI) and represents an emerging threat to last-resort carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) therapy. The extent to which co-carried resistance genes and clonal background modulate the CAZ-AVI resistance phenotype in KPC-31-producing organisms remains poorly defined.
Methods. Forty-two KPC-31-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae (n=33, 78.6%) and Escherichia coli (n=9, 21.4%) isolates underwent whole-genome sequencing (WGS), multilocus sequence typing (MLST), plasmid incompatibility group typing, and comprehensive antimicrobial susceptibility testing (MIC determination for 26 agents including CAZ-AVI and meropenem).
Results. All 42 isolates (100%) carried blaKPC-31. Five sequence types (STs) were identified: ST307 (n=16, 50.0%), ST101 (n=7, 21.9%), ST512 (n=5, 15.6%), ST147 (n=2, 6.3%), and ST131 (n=2, 6.3%). CAZ-AVI resistance (MIC >16 mg/L) was detected in 35.7% of isolates and was universal in ST101, ST512, and ST147, but absent or intermediate in 50% of ST307. Paradoxically, ST307 carried the highest burden of additional β-lactamase genes — blaSHV-28 (13/16 isolates, 81.3%) and blaCTX-M-15 (10/16, 62.5%) — yet exhibited the lowest median CAZ-AVI MIC (18 mg/L) among K. pneumoniae clones. Thirteen additional β-lactamase genes were identified across the collection; 45% of isolates carried none beyond blaKPC-31. IncX3 plasmids were exclusively associated with ST512 (5/5), while IncF-family plasmids were detected across four distinct STs, signalling active horizontal gene transfer. armA-mediated pan-aminoglycoside resistance was identified in ST101, and fosA in ST147, further restricting therapeutic options in these lineages.
Conclusions. Resistance phenotype in KPC-31-producing Enterobacterales is fundamentally shaped by clonal background rather than β-lactamase gene burden alone. The ST307 paradox — high gene burden with low MIC — likely reflects chromosomal integration of blaKPC-31 with attenuated expression. These findings demonstrate that WGS-based genotypic prediction cannot replace phenotypic MIC testing and underscore the need for integrated genomic and susceptibility surveillance in the clinical management of CRE infections.
Keywords: Klebsiella pneumoniae; KPC-31; ceftazidime-avibactam resistance; carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales; whole-genome sequencing; genotype-phenotype; sequence type 307

title: Genomic and phenotypic characterization of KPC-31-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli: convergence of high-risk clones and complex genotype-phenotype relationships
text:
Collection overview and species distribution
A total of 42 carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales isolates were characterized, comprising 33 Klebsiella pneumoniae (78.6%) and 9 Escherichia coli (21.4%). All 42 isolates (100%) carried blaKPC-31, confirming the clonal or epidemic nature of this collection. Multilocus sequence typing (MLST) identified five distinct sequence types among the 32 typed isolates: ST307 (n=16, 50.0%), ST101 (n=7, 21.9%), ST512 (n=5, 15.6%), ST147 (n=2, 6.3%), and ST131 (n=2, 6.3%; E. coli only). All four K. pneumoniae STs are recognized as globally disseminated high-risk clones.

title: Genomic and phenotypic characterization of KPC-31-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli: convergence of high-risk clones and complex genotype-phenotype relationships
text:
CAZ-AVI susceptibility and MIC distributions
CAZ-AVI MIC values varied substantially across the collection. Using a susceptibility breakpoint of ≤8 mg/L, 35.7% of isolates (n=15) demonstrated high-level resistance (MIC >16 mg/L), while 50.0% were susceptible. CAZ-AVI resistance was strongly associated with sequence type: ST512 (100%), ST147 (100%), and ST101 (100%) isolates were uniformly resistant, with median MICs of 48, 256, and 130 mg/L, respectively. ST307 showed marked heterogeneity, with approximately equal proportions of intermediate and susceptible phenotypes and a median MIC of 12 mg/L—substantially lower than the other K. pneumoniae clones, despite ST307 carrying the highest burden of additional β-lactamase genes.

title: Genomic and phenotypic characterization of KPC-31-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli: convergence of high-risk clones and complex genotype-phenotype relationships
section: Resistome: β-lactamase gene prevalence and burden
text:
Resistome: β-lactamase gene prevalence and burden
Excluding the universal blaKPC-31, 13 additional β-lactamase genes were identified across the collection. The most prevalent were blaSHV-28 (n=14, 33.3%), an ESBL predominantly carried by K. pneumoniae, and blaCTX-M-15 (n=11, 26.2%), exclusive to K. pneumoniae in this collection. blaOXA-1 was detected in 23.8% of isolates (n=10), and narrow-spectrum TEM-family enzymes (blaTEM-1A, blaTEM-1B) were present in 16.7% and 11.9% of isolates, respectively.
Gene burden analysis revealed a bimodal distribution: 45% of isolates (n=19) carried no additional β-lactamase genes beyond blaKPC-31, while 19% harbored four or more additional genes. One isolate carried six additional β-lactamase genes, representing the maximum gene burden in this collection. This bimodal pattern suggests two ecologically distinct strategies: reliance on blaKPC-31 alone versus extensive resistance gene acquisition. The complete resistome profile across all isolates, grouped by sequence type and resistance class, is shown in Figure 1.








Figure 1: Resistome heatmap of all 42 KPC-31-producing isolates, faceted by sequence type. Each row represents one isolate; each column represents one resistance gene. Dark cells indicate gene presence; light cells indicate absence. Genes are ordered left to right by resistance class (indicated by vertical dividers): carbapenemase | ESBL | narrow-spectrum β-lactamase | aminoglycoside | quinolone | sulfonamide | trimethoprim | tetracycline | macrolide | fosfomycin. The concentrated ESBL signal in ST307, the sparse but armA-positive profile of ST101, and the broad multi-class resistome of ST131 are clearly apparent.

title: Genomic and phenotypic characterization of KPC-31-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli: convergence of high-risk clones and complex genotype-phenotype relationships
text:
Gene combination effects
Analysis of gene co-carriage revealed context-dependent, non-additive effects on CAZ-AVI MIC. Isolates carrying blaCTX-M-15 together with blaTEM family enzymes showed lower median MICs (~12 mg/L), consistent with the predominantly ST307 background of these strains. By contrast, the highest median MICs were observed in isolates carrying blaSHV variants in non-ST307 clonal backgrounds, underscoring that the same gene combination produces distinct phenotypic outcomes depending on the broader genomic context.

title: Genomic and phenotypic characterization of KPC-31-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae and Escherichia coli: convergence of high-risk clones and complex genotype-phenotype relationships
text:
Plasmid incompatibility groups
Fifteen incompatibility (Inc) groups were detected. The IncF family (IncFIB(K), IncFII(K), IncFIB(pQil)) was the most prevalent, with IncF plasmids detected across four distinct sequence types, indicating active horizontal gene transfer (HGT) within the K. pneumoniae population. IncX3 plasmids were exclusively identified in ST512 isolates (100% within-clone prevalence), consistent with the established role of IncX3 as the predominant vehicle for blaKPC in this lineage. Notably, 62% of isolates—predominantly ST307—lacked detectable Inc groups, raising the possibility of chromosomal integration of blaKPC-31 in this clone, with potential implications for expression level and resistance phenotype.
